claims.text: The initial material is as-cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has a density of approximately 10.21 g cm^-3.
As-cast HfMoTaTiZr has robust mechanical performance at room and elevated temperatures.
Replacing the equiatomic Mo fraction with Nb produces equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Mo-to-Nb substitution will reduce the alloy density.
Mo-to-Nb substitution will preserve high strength at room temperature.
Mo-to-Nb substitution will preserve high-temperature mechanical performance at approximately 1000 °C.
The modified HfNbTaTiZr alloy will retain a BCC solid-solution microstructure.
The modified alloy will retain lattice distortion similar to that of HfMoTaTiZr.
The modified alloy will retain similar barriers to dislocation mobility.
Lattice distortion and dislocation-mobility barriers underlie the room- and high-temperature strength of these alloys.
Nb has a density of approximately 8.57 g cm^-3, compared with approximately 10.28 g cm^-3 for Mo.
Nb offers high-temperature BCC phase stability comparable to Mo in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The alloy-density decrease will be proportional to the atomic-mass difference between Nb and Mo.
The density of HfNbTaTiZr may be 5–10% lower than that of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr.
Yield strength and creep resistance will be maintained within acceptable limits from room temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
Prior work tested equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in room-temperature tension and compression and in creep at 982 °C under 120 and 200 MPa.
The hypothesis is intended to apply to tensile, compressive, and creep loading from ambient temperature to approximately 1000 °C.
The comparison will use vacuum-arc-melted HfNbTaTiZr and an as-cast HfMoTaTiZr control processed under identical conditions.
The hypothesis is rejected if density decreases by less than 5% or if yield strength or creep resistance decreases by more than 10% relative to HfMoTaTiZr.

contradictions.description: The stated boundary covers tensile, compressive, and creep behavior across room temperature through approximately 1000 °C, but the proposed measurements specify tensile and compression tests only at room temperature and creep only near 1000 °C. Thus, high-temperature tensile/compressive performance is claimed but not directly tested.

The rejection rule refers to yield strength or creep resistance at both room temperature and approximately 1000 °C, whereas the listed measurements do not include high-temperature yield strength or room-temperature creep resistance.
